classification.difficultyReason: Requires a parameter condition for global monotonicity and justification that isolated stationary points at the boundary values preserve one-to-one behaviour.

content.prompt: Let $f(x)=x^3+tx^2+x-1$. Find the range of values of the constant $t$ so that $f^{-1}$ exists.

inlines.text: to be nonnegative. Equality gives only an isolated stationary point.

answer.worked:
An inverse exists exactly when $f$ is one-to-one. Since this cubic tends to $-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ and to $\infty$ as $x\to\infty$, it must be strictly increasing to be one-to-one.

$$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=3x^2+2tx+1\\f'(x)&=3\left(x+\frac{t}{3}\right)^2+1-\frac{t^2}{3}\end{align*}$$

Thus $f'(x)\ge0$ for every real $x$ exactly when

$$\begin{align*}1-\frac{t^2}{3}&\ge0\\t^2&\le3\\-\sqrt{3}&\le t\le\sqrt{3}.\end{align*}$$

For these values, $f$ is strictly increasing: at $t=\pm\sqrt{3}$, the derivative vanishes at only one point. If $|t|>\sqrt{3}$, the derivative changes sign, giving turning points, so $f$ is not one-to-one. Therefore $\boxed{-\sqrt{3}\le t\le\sqrt{3}}$.
